title: Sulfites in Wine: Do They Really Cause Headaches?
excerpt: What sulfites in wine are, why winemakers add them, what 'Contains Sulfites' means, and what the evidence says about headaches, including the better suspects and whether natural wine helps.
metaDescription: What are sulfites in wine, and do they cause headaches? What the evidence says, the likelier culprits (quercetin, histamine), and if natural wine helps.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most people, sulfites are not the reason wine gives them a headache. Sulfite sensitivity is real, but it mostly causes breathing problems (wheezing and chest tightness), usually in people with asthma. Headache has never been shown to be a typical sulfite reaction. White wine generally contains more sulfites than red, yet red wine is the one people blame. Dried apricots can hold many times more sulfite than a glass of wine and rarely get blamed for headaches at all. The better-supported suspects are the alcohol itself, how much of it you drink, and compounds concentrated in red grape skins, especially a flavonoid called **quercetin**, along with histamine and other by-products of fermentation.

This guide explains what sulfites actually are, why winemakers use them, what the "Contains Sulfites" label really means, what the research says about sulfites and headaches, what the better suspects are, and whether "natural" or sulfite-free wine is worth trying.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general research and labeling rules. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor or allergist if** you get wheezing, chest tightness, hives, throat or lip swelling, or trouble breathing after wine or other sulfite-containing foods, especially if you have asthma. **Call 911 or your local emergency number** for any sudden trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or fainting. If you have frequent or severe headaches, or headaches that have changed in pattern, talk to your doctor rather than assuming wine is the only trigger.

## What Are Sulfites in Wine?

"Sulfites" is the everyday name for a group of sulfur-based compounds. In wine the main one is **sulfur dioxide (SO2)**, which winemakers add as a gas, as a liquid solution, or as a powder called potassium metabisulfite. Once in the wine, it settles into a balance of related forms. Some of it stays "free," which is the active, protective part, and some of it binds to other molecules in the wine.

### Why winemakers add them

Sulfites do two jobs that are hard to replace:

- **They stop spoilage.** Grape juice is full of sugar and is a natural home for wild yeasts and bacteria. Sulfites hold back the microbes that would turn wine into vinegar or give it off-flavors, while the wine yeast the winemaker wants can still do its job.
- **They slow oxidation.** Oxygen turns wine brown, flat, and stale, a bit like a cut apple left on the counter. Sulfites act as an antioxidant and protect the fruit flavors and color, especially in wine meant to be shipped, stored, or aged.

Wine has been treated with sulfur for centuries. Burning sulfur inside empty barrels to keep them clean is an old practice, so sulfites are not a modern industrial shortcut, even if they are now measured and controlled far more precisely.

### Some sulfites are made by the yeast itself

Even if a winemaker adds nothing, yeast produces small amounts of sulfites naturally while it ferments sugar into alcohol. That's why there is essentially no such thing as a completely sulfite-free wine. "No sulfites added" is accurate on some labels; "sulfite-free" usually isn't.

### Sulfites are in plenty of foods, too

Wine is far from the biggest source of sulfites in a typical diet. They're widely used to preserve:

- **Dried fruit**, especially light-colored fruit like dried apricots and golden raisins, which can contain many times more sulfite than wine
- **Some processed potatoes**, bottled lemon and lime juice, pickled foods, and certain jams
- **Some shrimp and other shellfish**, to prevent black spots
- **Molasses, some vinegars, and some condiments**

This matters for the headache question. If sulfites were a common headache trigger, a handful of dried apricots should be more of a problem than a glass of wine. For most people, it isn't.

## How Much Sulfite Is in Wine?

Sulfite levels are measured in milligrams per liter (mg/L), which is the same as parts per million (ppm). A few useful reference points:

- **The US legal maximum for wine is 350 ppm.** Most wines sit well below that.
- **The European Union sets lower limits that vary by style.** Dry red wines are allowed the least, dry whites and rosés a bit more, and sweet wines more still, because residual sugar gives microbes more to feed on and needs more protection.
- **Red wines generally contain less sulfite than white wines.** Tannins and other compounds from red grape skins act as natural antioxidants, so reds need less added protection. Sweet white wines tend to have the most.
- **Organic and "natural" wines usually contain less.** In the US, wine labeled simply "organic" under USDA rules cannot have added sulfites at all. Wine "made with organic grapes" can contain added sulfites up to a lower limit than conventional wine.

The red-versus-white point is the single biggest problem for the sulfite theory of wine headaches. People most often blame **red** wine for headaches, and red wine usually has **less** sulfite.

## What Does "Contains Sulfites" on a Label Mean?

In the United States, federal rules require the statement "Contains Sulfites" on any wine with **10 ppm or more** of sulfur dioxide. That threshold is low enough that nearly every wine qualifies, since yeast alone can produce amounts in that range.

The labeling rule came about in the 1980s after reports of serious reactions in sulfite-sensitive people, most of them with asthma. Around the same time, the FDA banned sulfites on fresh fruits and vegetables meant to be eaten raw, such as salad-bar produce, which had been treated heavily to keep it looking fresh.

So the warning exists to protect a small group of people who are genuinely sensitive. It's an allergen-style notice, not a sign that a wine is unusually high in sulfites, and not evidence that sulfites cause headaches. Many European wines carry a similar "contains sulphites" notice, and wines sold in the US but imported from elsewhere carry the US statement. Wines from many other countries don't carry any notice at all, which is one reason people sometimes believe "European wines don't have sulfites" (they do).

## Sulfite Sensitivity Is Real, but It Mostly Affects Breathing

Some people genuinely react to sulfites. Here's what the reaction usually looks like:

- **Who it affects:** mostly people with asthma. Estimates vary, but medical reviews generally describe it as affecting a minority of people with asthma and well under 1 to 2 percent of the general population.
- **What it does:** the classic reaction is **wheezing, coughing, and chest tightness**, sometimes within minutes. Less often, people get flushing, hives, itching, stomach upset, or a drop in blood pressure. Severe reactions are rare but can be serious.
- **Why it happens:** in many cases it isn't a true allergy in the classic sense. One leading explanation is that sulfur dioxide released from the food or drink irritates the airways directly, which twitchy, asthmatic airways respond to strongly. Some people may also have trouble breaking sulfites down.

Notice what's missing from that list: **headache**. Headache is not one of the recognized hallmark symptoms of sulfite sensitivity. That doesn't mean no one ever gets a headache from sulfites, but it does mean the common belief that "wine headaches = sulfite allergy" isn't supported by how sulfite reactions actually present.

### The dried-fruit test

A simple, low-tech clue: if you eat dried apricots, golden raisins, or other sulfured dried fruit without any trouble, sulfites in wine are unlikely to be your problem, because those foods generally contain far more sulfite per serving than a glass of wine. This isn't a medical test, and if you have asthma or a history of serious reactions you shouldn't experiment on your own. But for most people it's a useful reality check.

If you think you're genuinely sulfite-sensitive, an allergist can confirm it, usually with a supervised challenge test in a clinic where any reaction can be treated.

## What the Research Says About Sulfites and Headaches

The honest summary: **the link between sulfites and headaches is weak, and researchers who study wine headaches mostly look elsewhere.**

A few points from the research and clinical literature:

- **Reviews of alcohol and headache don't single out sulfites.** Reviews of alcohol as a migraine and headache trigger, including a widely cited 2008 review in *The Journal of Headache and Pain*, discuss sulfites mostly to note that the evidence linking them to headache is weak. Alcohol itself, histamine, tyramine, and flavonoids get more attention.
- **Red wine is the bigger headache trigger, despite having fewer sulfites.** In a small British study published in *The Lancet* in the late 1980s, people with migraine who believed red wine was a trigger were given either red wine or a vodka drink matched for alcohol. A number of them developed migraine after the red wine and none after the vodka. Neither drink was tested for sulfites as the cause, but the result points to something specific to red wine beyond alcohol, and red wine is the lower-sulfite option.
- **People who report wine intolerance describe a mix of symptoms.** A 2012 survey from Mainz, Germany, published in *Deutsches Ärzteblatt International*, found that a meaningful minority of adults reported intolerance reactions to wine, most commonly flushing, itching, and nasal congestion as well as headache, and more often after red wine. Surveys like this can't identify the cause, but the pattern fits better with red-wine compounds than with sulfites.

None of this proves sulfites never contribute. It does mean that blaming them first, and then switching to expensive "sulfite-free" wine, is often aiming at the wrong target.

## The Better Suspects

If not sulfites, then what? Here are the explanations with more support, roughly from strongest to most speculative.

### 1. The alcohol itself (and how much of it)

This is the boring answer, and it's the most important one. Alcohol on its own can cause headaches in several ways: it widens blood vessels, it makes you lose more fluid than you take in, it disrupts sleep, and the body turns it into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound linked to many hangover symptoms. A large glass of wine often holds more alcohol than people assume, and wines have grown stronger over the decades. A 14.5% red poured into a big glass can easily be close to two standard drinks.

Our guide to [why alcohol causes headaches](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) explains these mechanisms in more detail.

### 2. Quercetin and the acetaldehyde bottleneck

The most interesting recent idea comes from researchers at the University of California, Davis. In a 2023 study published in *Scientific Reports*, they screened compounds found in red wine and found that a form of **quercetin** (quercetin glucuronide, which is what quercetin becomes after your body processes it) can block **ALDH2**, the main enzyme that clears acetaldehyde.

If that enzyme is partly blocked, acetaldehyde can build up, which is the same basic mechanism behind the facial flushing, headache, and nausea that many people of East Asian heritage experience when they drink (see our [guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive)).

Why does this fit the red-wine pattern?

- Quercetin is concentrated in **grape skins**, and red wine is made with long skin contact, while most white wine is not.
- Quercetin levels vary a lot between wines. Grapes grown with more sun exposure tend to have more, and winemaking choices change how much ends up in the bottle. That could explain why one red gives you a headache and another doesn't.
- The headache often shows up within a few hours of drinking a modest amount, which is more consistent with an acetaldehyde effect than with dehydration.

**An important caveat:** this was a lab study, not a trial in people. The researchers themselves described it as a hypothesis that needs to be tested in human drinkers. It's a strong lead, not a settled answer.

### 3. Histamine and other biogenic amines

Wine, especially red wine, contains **histamine** and related compounds called biogenic amines (including **tyramine**), which form during fermentation, partly through the bacteria involved in the secondary "malolactic" fermentation that softens many reds. Histamine can widen blood vessels and cause flushing, a stuffy nose, and headache.

Most people break down dietary histamine easily with an enzyme in the gut called **diamine oxidase (DAO)**. Some people seem to have lower DAO activity, a pattern often called **histamine intolerance**, and alcohol may interfere with histamine breakdown as well.

The evidence here is genuinely mixed. A 2001 study in the *Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology* gave people who reported wine intolerance wines with low and high histamine content and found no clear link between histamine levels and their symptoms. Other researchers think histamine may matter for a subset of people. So histamine is a reasonable suspect, especially if your reaction includes flushing and a blocked nose, but it isn't proven to be the main cause for most people.

### 4. Congeners and tannins

**Congeners** are the many by-products of fermentation and aging other than ethanol, including methanol, other alcohols, and various flavor compounds. Dark drinks such as red wine, bourbon, and brandy contain more of them than clear drinks like vodka or white wine. Research comparing high-congener and low-congener drinks (bourbon versus vodka, for example) has found that higher-congener drinks tend to produce somewhat worse hangovers at the same alcohol dose. Our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) goes deeper.

**Tannins**, the compounds that make red wine feel dry and grippy, have also been proposed as a migraine trigger because they may affect serotonin, a brain chemical involved in migraine. The evidence for tannins specifically is thin, and many foods high in tannins (strong tea, dark chocolate) don't bother most people.

### 5. Context: dehydration, sleep, and everything else

Wine is often drunk with long dinners, late nights, salty food, and not much water. Poor sleep alone is a strong headache trigger. Before you blame any single compound, it's worth asking how much you drank, how fast, how much water you had, and how well you slept.

For a fuller look at why red wine in particular seems to cause headaches, see our companion piece on the [red wine headache](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache), and our broader [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) for how wine hangovers differ from other drinks.

## Natural Wine, Organic Wine, and "Sulfite-Free" Wine

Natural wine has become popular partly on the promise that it won't cause headaches or hangovers. Here's what's actually going on.

### What the labels mean

- **"Natural wine"** has no legal definition in the US. It usually means organically farmed grapes, wild (native) yeast, few or no additives, little or no filtering, and little or no added sulfite. In France, a voluntary "Vin Méthode Nature" certification allows a small amount of added sulfite at bottling and none before.
- **"Organic wine"** (USDA certified) means organic grapes and **no added sulfites**. Natural sulfites from fermentation are still present.
- **"Made with organic grapes"** means organic grapes but allows some added sulfites, within a lower limit than conventional wine.
- **"No sulfites added"** means the winemaker didn't add any. The wine still contains the small amount the yeast produced.

### Does natural wine prevent headaches?

There's no good research showing it does. The reasoning goes like this:

- **If sulfites aren't your trigger, removing them won't help.** For most people, they aren't.
- **Natural wines aren't automatically lower in the better suspects.** A natural red still has skin-derived compounds like quercetin. Spontaneous fermentation and minimal intervention can also mean more variable levels of histamine and other biogenic amines, though this varies widely from bottle to bottle.
- **Some natural wines are lighter and lower in alcohol.** Many are made in a fresh, low-alcohol style. If a natural wine is 11% instead of 14.5%, and you drink the same number of glasses, you're simply drinking less alcohol. That alone can explain why some people feel better.
- **People often drink natural wine differently.** It's frequently served in smaller pours, at wine bars with food, or in more relaxed settings. Context changes how much and how fast you drink.

None of this means natural wine is bad. Many people love it for its flavor. Just don't pay a premium for it on the belief that it's a headache cure, and if you try it, compare like with like: the same amount of alcohol, the same water, the same sleep.

## A Practical Way to Find Your Real Trigger

Instead of guessing, run a simple personal experiment over a few weeks. Keep a short note of what you drank, how much, how strong it was, whether you ate, how much water you had, and how you felt the next day.

1. **Measure your pours.** A standard US drink of wine is 5 ounces (about 150 ml) at 12% alcohol. Many home pours are much bigger. Note the alcohol percentage on the label; the difference between 12% and 15% is meaningful.
2. **Compare red and white at the same dose.** If dry white wine (usually higher in sulfites) is fine and red isn't, sulfites are unlikely to be the issue.
3. **Try the dried-fruit check.** If sulfured dried fruit doesn't bother you, wine sulfites probably won't either. Skip this if you have asthma or a history of reactions.
4. **Try different reds.** Lighter reds, such as Pinot Noir or Gamay, can behave differently from heavier, sun-ripened, high-alcohol reds. If some reds are fine and others aren't, that points toward compounds that vary between wines (like quercetin or histamine), not toward red wine in general.
5. **Keep everything else steady.** Eat a proper meal, alternate each glass with water, and stop at a set number.

If your symptoms include wheezing, chest tightness, hives, or swelling, stop experimenting and talk to a doctor or allergist.

## How to Reduce Wine Headaches (What Actually Helps)

These steps address the explanations with the best support:

- **Drink less, and drink slower.** The dose of alcohol is the strongest predictor of how you'll feel. Pacing to roughly one drink per hour gives your body more time to clear acetaldehyde.
- **Choose lower-alcohol wines.** Look for wines around 11 to 12.5% rather than 14 to 15%.
- **Eat before and while drinking.** Food slows how fast alcohol is absorbed.
- **Alternate with water.** One glass of water for each glass of wine helps with dehydration and naturally slows your pace.
- **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can.
- **If red wine is a consistent trigger, switch styles.** Try lighter reds, whites, or a different drink altogether. Our [ranking of the drinks least likely to give you a hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) is a useful place to start.

### What about antihistamines?

Some people who suspect histamine take an antihistamine before drinking wine. There's limited evidence this prevents wine headaches, and some antihistamines cause drowsiness that alcohol makes much worse. Don't combine sedating antihistamines with alcohol, and check with a pharmacist or doctor before trying any medicine alongside drinking.

### What about painkillers the next morning?

If you wake up with a headache, painkillers can help, but each has its own risks after drinking. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) adds work for the liver, and ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate a stomach already irritated by alcohol. Read our guides to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [fast relief for a hangover headache](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) before reaching for anything.

### Where DHM fits

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol, mostly in animals. A 2012 study in *The Journal of Neuroscience* found that it reduced signs of alcohol intoxication in rats, and other lab research suggests it may support the body's handling of alcohol and acetaldehyde. Human evidence is still limited, and there's no research showing DHM prevents wine headaches specifically. It doesn't affect sulfites or histamine, and it isn't a substitute for drinking less.

If you want to try it as one part of a sensible plan, two widely used options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [guide to preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## When to See a Doctor

Wine headaches are usually a nuisance, not a danger. But get medical advice if:

- You get **wheezing, chest tightness, coughing fits, hives, or swelling** after wine or sulfite-containing foods. Get emergency help for trouble breathing or swelling of the face or throat.
- You have **asthma** and suspect sulfites are making it worse.
- Your headaches are **frequent, severe, or getting worse**, or come with vision changes, weakness, numbness, confusion, or a stiff neck.
- You get headaches or flushing after **very small amounts** of alcohol, which can point to a problem with how your body processes alcohol.
- You find you're using painkillers regularly to recover from drinking.

## The Bottom Line

- **Sulfites are preservatives** (mostly sulfur dioxide) that protect wine from spoilage and oxidation. Yeast makes some naturally, so virtually all wine contains them.
- **Sulfite sensitivity is real but uncommon**, mostly affects people with asthma, and mainly causes breathing symptoms, not headaches.
- **White wine usually has more sulfites than red**, and dried fruit has far more than wine, which makes sulfites a poor explanation for the "red wine headache."
- **Better suspects** are the alcohol dose itself, quercetin from red grape skins (which may slow acetaldehyde clearance), histamine and other biogenic amines, and congeners. The quercetin idea is promising but still being tested in people.
- **Natural and sulfite-free wines** aren't proven to prevent headaches. If they help you, lower alcohol content and drinking pattern may be the reason.
- **What reliably helps:** smaller pours, lower-alcohol wines, food, water, sleep, and finding your personal trigger with a simple diary.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do sulfites in wine cause headaches?**

For most people, probably not. Sulfite sensitivity is real, but it mainly causes breathing symptoms such as wheezing and chest tightness, usually in people with asthma. Headache has never been shown to be a reliable sulfite reaction, and white wine usually contains more sulfites than red, even though red wine is the one people blame for headaches. Alcohol itself, the amount you drink, and compounds in red grape skins (such as quercetin) are more likely culprits.

**What are sulfites in wine and why are they added?**

Sulfites are sulfur-based compounds, mostly sulfur dioxide, that protect wine from spoiling. They stop unwanted bacteria and wild yeast from growing and slow down oxidation, which would otherwise turn wine brown and flat. Yeast also makes small amounts of sulfites naturally during fermentation, so almost no wine is completely sulfite-free.

**Does red wine have more sulfites than white wine?**

Usually not. Dry red wines generally contain fewer sulfites than dry white, rose, and especially sweet white wines, because the tannins in red wine help protect it from oxidation. EU rules reflect this by allowing a lower maximum for dry reds than for dry whites. That is one of the main reasons researchers doubt sulfites explain the 'red wine headache.'

**What does 'Contains Sulfites' on a wine label mean?**

In the US, any wine with 10 parts per million (ppm) or more of sulfites must carry the 'Contains Sulfites' statement. The rule exists to protect the small group of people who are truly sensitive, most of whom have asthma. It is not a sign that the wine is unusually high in sulfites; nearly every wine qualifies, because yeast alone can produce close to that amount.

**Is natural wine better for avoiding headaches?**

There is no good evidence that it is. Natural wines are usually made with little or no added sulfite, but if sulfites are not what causes your headaches, removing them will not help. Some natural wines are lower in alcohol, which can help, while others may carry more histamine and other compounds from spontaneous fermentation. Judge it by how you feel, and keep the amount you drink the same when you compare.

**How do I know if I am sensitive to sulfites?**

Sulfite sensitivity usually shows up as wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, or a flushed, itchy feeling soon after eating or drinking something high in sulfites, and it is much more common in people with asthma. A useful clue: dried apricots and other dried fruits typically contain far more sulfites than wine. If those do not bother you, sulfites in wine are unlikely to be your problem. An allergist can confirm it with a supervised challenge test.

**Why does red wine give me a headache but white wine does not?**

The leading explanations involve compounds that are concentrated in red grape skins, not sulfites. A 2023 lab study from UC Davis found that a form of quercetin, a flavonoid in red wine, can block one of the enzymes that clears acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol. Red wine also tends to carry more histamine and other congeners. These ideas are still being tested in people, so treat them as strong suspects rather than proven causes.

**Can I remove sulfites from wine?**

Products such as sulfite-removing drops and filter wands use a small amount of hydrogen peroxide or a resin to bind free sulfites, and they can lower sulfite levels. They are a reasonable tool if you have confirmed sulfite sensitivity. But since sulfites are not a proven cause of wine headaches, most people will not notice a difference in headaches from using them. If you have asthma and react to sulfites, do not rely on these products in place of your doctor's advice.
